text_blocks.snippet: When a bond's yield to maturity (YTM) is less than its coupon rate, the bond is selling at a premium. This means the bond's market price is higher than its face value.
snippet_highlighted_words: the bond is selling at a premium

list.title: Higher Interest Payments:
list.snippet: A bond with a lower YTM indicates that investors are willing to accept a lower return than the coupon rate suggests. This typically happens when the bond's interest payments are more attractive than those of newly issued bonds in the current market.

list.title: Increased Demand:
list.snippet: Because the bond offers a higher coupon rate than what is currently available in the market, demand for that bond increases, pushing its price up.

list.title: Premium Price:
list.snippet: As a result of the increased demand and higher price, the bond trades at a premium to its face value.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, when a bond's YTM is lower than its coupon rate, it's a sign that the bond is a good deal for investors, and they are willing to pay more to own it.
